questions.question: For a row-stochastic bonus-malus transition matrix P, the row vector z of all zeros satisfies zP=z. Why is z not a stationary distribution?
options: Its entries must all be strictly positive.
Its entries do not sum to one.
Its invariant equation needs Pz rather than zP.
Its entries must equal the class premiums.

questions.question: A finite bonus-malus chain may be periodic. Its initial class law is a stationary row distribution pi, so pi P=pi. Must its class law change in later years because aperiodicity was not assumed?
options: Yes; invariance for one year is lost after a second transition.
Yes; periodicity forces every initial distribution to oscillate.
No; starting stationary makes the transition matrix irreducible.
No; a stationary start stays invariant after every transition.

questions.question: A row-stochastic bonus-malus matrix has rows (0.9,0.1),(0.2,0.8). An analyst calls row (0.5,0.5) stationary because the same weights as a column are unchanged by P. Is that proof valid for the row law?
options: No; multiplying the row by P gives (0.55,0.45), which differs.
Yes; a column calculation also proves invariance of the same row.
Yes; equal class weights are stationary for every row-stochastic P.
No; every stationary row must equal the first transition row.

questions.question: A bonus-malus insurer changes class prices but retains exactly the same transition matrix P and a unique stationary law. What happens to stationary class probabilities?
options: They rise in every class whose price rises.
They become proportional to class prices.
They remain unchanged.
They must be recomputed from the price ratios alone.

questions.question: All classes with positive stationary probability have prices strictly between 100 and 200 euros. What must hold for their stationary mean premium b?
A two-class transition matrix has rows (0.8,0.2) and (0.3,0.7). What is its stationary row distribution?
Stationary probabilities of three classes are (0.2,0.16,0.64), with prices (200,200,100) euros. What is the stationary mean premium?
options: 164 euros.
500/3 euros.
136 euros.
100 euros.

questions.question: For the three-class identity transition matrix, the invariant row vector (1.2,-0.2,0) sums to one. Is it a stationary distribution?
options: No; it assigns negative probability to the second class.
Yes; invariance and unit sum are sufficient.
No; the zero third entry violates stationarity.
Yes; negative entries represent premium discounts.

questions.question: In the two-year scheme, P has rows $(p,q,0),(p,0,q),(p,0,q)$ with $p=1-\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda}$, $q=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda}$. At $\lambda=0$, what stationary law follows?
A stationary class law is fixed. Every class price is increased by seven euros. If the old mean premium was 120 euros, what is the new mean?
options: 120 euros.
141 euros for three classes.
840 euros.
127 euros.

questions.question: For row-stochastic P, let a row vector x solve all but one coordinate equation of xP=x. Why does the omitted balance equation follow, without making normalisation automatic?
options: The omitted equation follows only when class premiums are equal.
The retained equations force every coordinate of x to be positive.
The coordinate residuals sum to zero, but x can still have arbitrary total mass.
The omitted equation determines total mass one independently of the others.

questions.question: The two-year scheme has P rows $(p,q,0),(p,0,q),(p,0,q)$, with $0<p,q<1$, $p+q=1$. Classes 1,2 both cost c and class 3 costs a<c. Why can merging classes 1,2 preserve a mean price yet lose the transition information?
options: Equal prices hide different next-year chances of reaching class 3.
Their prices agree, so their transitions must agree as well.
Equal current prices require equal stationary weights for the two classes.
Only current mean pricing is lost; next-year transitions remain fully specified.

questions.question: A chain charges exactly 100 euros in every class. Its expected premium is therefore 100 euros at every year. Does this constant mean demonstrate that its class distribution is stationary?
options: Yes; a constant weighted mean identifies every class probability.
Yes; constant prices imply every transition row is identical.
No; stationary laws require different prices in different classes.
No; different changing class laws all give the same price.

questions.question: In the two-year scheme p=0.2, q=0.8 and P has rows (p,q,0),(p,0,q),(p,0,q). Starting in class 1 with certainty, what is the distribution after exactly two transitions?
A two-year scheme has high price c=200, low price a=100 and $b(\lambda)=c+(a-c)\mathrm{e}^{-2\lambda}$ for claim rate $\lambda\ge0$. If its stationary mean is 150, what rate is implied?
options: $\lambda=\log2$.
$\lambda=(\log2)/2$.
$\lambda=2\log2$.
$\lambda=1/2$.

questions.question: Stationary probabilities are (0.2,0.3,0.5). Only the second class price is raised by 20 euros; transitions remain fixed. By how much does the stationary mean premium rise?
options: 6 euros.
20 euros.
10 euros.
4 euros.

questions.question: A two-class chain deterministically switches class each year. Its transition rows are (0,1),(1,0), and prices are 100,200 euros. What disproves convergence from every initial law despite its unique stationary law?
options: Starting in class 1 gives the stationary premium 150 every year.
The vector(1/2,1/2) fails the balance equation.
Starting in class 1 gives alternating laws and premiums 100,200.
The two concentrated class laws are both stationary.

questions.question: A three-class chain never changes class: P is the identity. Prices are 100,150,200 euros. Does a stationary mean premium 150 identify a unique stationary distribution?
options: Yes; only the middle class can contribute to a mean 150.
No; both(0,1,0) and(1/2,0,1/2) are stationary with that mean.
Yes; normalisation makes an identity-chain law unique.
No; the identity matrix is inadmissible because stationarity requires a unique law.

questions.question: Let $\Lambda$ be the fixed claim rate of a uniformly sampled policyholder: half the cohort has rate 0 and half has rate $\log 2$. Each subgroup has two-year stationary premium $b(\lambda)=200-100\mathrm{e}^{-2\lambda}$. Compare the subgroup-price average with $b(\mathbb{E}[\Lambda])$.
options: They are 137.5 and 150 euros, respectively.
They are both 150 euros.
They are 150 and 137.5 euros, respectively.
They are both 137.5 euros.

questions.question: The two-year transition matrix has rows(p,q,0),(p,0,q),(p,0,q), with p the annual claim probability and q=1-p. The first year has p=0.2 and the second has p=0.5. From any initial law, what is the mean premium after these two transitions if class prices are 200,200,100?
options: 175 euros.
136 euros.
157.75 euros.
160 euros.
